catalog_quote: [p.51] Stress does not fall on the penultimate syllable, as is generally the case in Oceanic languages, but on the final syllable. Stress has a fairly low functional load at word-level. [...] [p.62, 2.1.3.2 Stress] In roots with two syllables, stressed is place on the final syllable. [...] /a.ˈo/ ‘yes’ [...] /tɔ.ˈbaŋ/ ‘basket’ [...] /tit.ˈmwo/ ‘rat’ [...] [p.63] In roots with three syllables, secondary stress is placed on the first syllable and primary stress remains on the final syllable. [...] /ˌta.ba.ˈria/ ‘house.spider’ [...] In four-syllable words, primary stress falls on the final syllable and secondary stress falls on the first syllable. [...] /ˌtao.raŋ.mi.ˈsior/ ‘July’ [...] In Ske, subject markers are pro-clitics which may cliticise on to a verb to form a phonological word and for stress assignment purposes they are handled accordingly. When pro-clitic and root are monosyllabic, a di-syllabic word sees stress assigned to the final syllable. [...] /ˌmwabɛ= ˈba/ ‘1PL.EXCL.IPFV=go’ [...] Nominalising affixes are monosyllabic and also form a phonological word with the root, thus primary stress is assigned to the suffix: [...] /ˌßa-ˈan/ ‘go-NMLZ’ ‘trip’ [...] [p.58] sequences of two vowels follow stress assignment patterns of Ske such that the final vowel is stressed, whereas with diphthongs, stress is placed on the first element. [...] /ˈao/ ‘rope’ /a.ˈo/ ‘yes’

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the phonological word (root, root+nominalising suffix, or subject-proclitic+verb); stress carries little functional load at word level.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of three- and four-syllable words (including proclitic+root combinations), e.g. /ˌta.ba.ˈria/, /ˌtao.raŋ.mi.ˈsior/, /ˌmwabɛ=ˈba/.
new_statements.exceptions: Transitivising -si and =ne attract primary stress only when the introduced argument is overt, which Johnson treats as phrase-level rather than word-level stress; otherwise the final syllable of the verb root is stressed (pp.63-64). An optional utterance-final echo vowel (/ˈskɔr/ -> [ˈskɔrɔ], p.66) does not take stress, so such tokens surface with penultimate stress; Johnson reads this as a residue of an earlier Oceanic-type penultimate pattern prior to final-vowel loss. She notes stress assignment is 'more complex than described here' (p.64).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word: subject proclitics and monosyllabic nominalising suffixes are included in the stress domain; examples are citation forms in a sketch-grammar chapter (impressionistic, no instrumental study). Phrase-level intonation discussed separately.
new_statements.identity_note: Johnson 2014 describes Ske (Seke) of south-western/south-central Pentecost centred on Baravet (Bwaravet) village = Glottolog seke1241, ISO ske; she reports no significant dialect variation. The extinct Doltes variety of Hotwata is not covered.

sources.note: Ch.2 sketch grammar, sec. 2.1 (p.51): stress falls on the final syllable, not the penult as generally in Oceanic; low functional load at word level. Sec. 2.1.3.2 'Stress' (pp.62-64): primary stress on final syllable of 2-,3-,4-syllable roots; secondary stress on first syllable of 3- and 4-syllable words; subject proclitic+verb forms one phonological word stressed the same way; monosyllabic nominalising suffixes take primary stress; transitivisers -si/=ne attract stress only at phrase level when the argument is overt. p.66: utterance-final echo vowel (/'skOr/ -> ['skOrO]) does not shift stress…
'Stress typically occurs on the final syllable of a word', footnoted to Johnson 2014 pp.62-64 (second-hand; used only to locate the primary source).
